claims.qualification: Records the GOV.UK publication only; the declaration's own text is a statement by the countries attending, not a UK instrument.

evidence.passage: Published: 1 November 2023

claims.subject: bletchley-declaration-2023

object.value: Describes the 'frontier' of AI as highly capable general-purpose AI models, including foundation models, and relevant specific narrow AI that could exhibit harmful capabilities, which match or exceed the capabilities of today's most advanced models.

claims.statement: The Bletchley Declaration describes the 'frontier' of AI as highly capable general-purpose AI models, including foundation models, that could perform a wide variety of tasks, together with relevant narrow AI that could exhibit harmful capabilities, matching or exceeding the most advanced models of the time.

time.note: Dated by the declaration’s publication on GOV.UK.

claims.qualification: A description in a non-binding declaration, not a legal definition; it sets no measurable threshold. Wording checked in the GOV.UK HTML as updated on 13 February 2025; the 2023 bytes were not inspected.

evidence.passage: Particular safety risks arise at the ‘frontier’ of AI, understood as being those highly capable general-purpose AI models, including foundation models, that could perform a wide variety of tasks
evidence.note: The same sentence continues with narrow AI and 'which match or exceed the capabilities present in today’s most advanced models'.

claims.subject: bletchley-declaration-2023

object.value: Affirms that actors developing frontier AI capabilities have a particularly strong responsibility for ensuring the safety of these systems, including through safety testing and evaluations.

claims.statement: The Bletchley Declaration affirms that actors developing frontier AI capabilities, in particular unusually powerful and potentially harmful systems, have a 'particularly strong responsibility' for ensuring their safety, including through safety testing and evaluations.
claims.qualification: An affirmation by the participating governments; it imposes no legal duty and names no developer.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning 'We affirm that, whilst safety must be considered across the AI lifecycle'
evidence.passage: actors developing frontier AI capabilities, in particular those AI systems which are unusually powerful and potentially harmful, have a particularly strong responsibility for ensuring the safety of these AI systems, including through systems for safety testing, through evaluations, and by other appropriate measures

claims.subject: bletchley-declaration-2023

object.value: Includes, within the agenda item on risk-based policies, increased transparency by private actors developing frontier AI capabilities.

claims.statement: The Bletchley Declaration's agenda for addressing frontier AI risk includes, under building risk-based policies, increased transparency by private actors developing frontier AI capabilities.
claims.qualification: An agenda item for participating governments, not a transparency obligation on any developer.

evidence.locator: Second agenda bullet ('building respective risk-based policies')
evidence.passage: alongside increased transparency by private actors developing frontier AI capabilities
evidence.note: The paragraph before also encourages 'all relevant actors' to provide context-appropriate transparency and accountability on plans to measure, monitor and mitigate harmful capabilities (paraphrase).

claims.subject: bletchley-chair-safety-testing-2023

object.value: Records the participants' acknowledgement that developers have responsibility to devise and conduct safety testing through evaluations, transparency and other appropriate measures.

claims.qualification: An acknowledgement reported by the chair, not a binding duty.

evidence.passage: Developers both have responsibility to devise and conduct safety testing through evaluations, transparency, and other appropriate measures

claims.subject: bletchley-chair-safety-testing-2023

object.value: Governments recognise an increasing role in seeing that external evaluations are undertaken for frontier AI models developed within their countries, before and after deployment.

evidence.passage: Governments recognise their increasing role for seeing that external evaluations are undertaken for frontier AI models developed within their countries
evidence.note: The point continues that the tests 'should be conducted before and after those models are deployed'.

openQuestions.question: Country subjects: the dataset has no country entity type, but listings (Bletchley, Paris, New Delhi) and absences have countries as subjects.
openQuestions.recommended: Add a 'country' entity type (or a public_body subtype 'state') with ISO 3166 codes; record per-country listings only where a claim needs them, and keep whole lists as one document-level listing claim as done here.

openQuestions.question: Proposed predicates used: lists_participants (document → literal list), not_listed (country → document), renamed_body (public_body → public_body).
openQuestions.recommended: Admit lists_participants as a document-level listing predicate with a required count basis ('stated' or 'counted'); model not_listed as a negative listing claim tied to a list snapshot date; model the renaming as a name-validity interval on the entity rather than a claim, if the schema supports names over time.

openQuestions.question: provision.kind value “principle” was used for non-binding affirmations (Bletchley, Seoul, chair’s statement), which fit none of the listed kinds.
openQuestions.recommended: Add “principle” (a non-binding affirmation or call) to the kind list. The two bounded-search records were moved by the integrator to provision_not_found with an inference rationale, as the dataset records absences in framework editions.

openQuestions.question: Intergovernmental bodies (G7, OECD) as publishers.
openQuestions.recommended: Use public_body with a subtype 'intergovernmental', distinct from national bodies.

openQuestions.question: Endorser counts for the New Delhi Declaration (88 on 21 February, 91 on 24 February, 92 as of 5 March 2026) and first-round counts for the HAIP reporting framework (19, 20 and 25 in three official descriptions) differ.
openQuestions.recommended: Integrator’s disposition (2026-10-28): neither is recorded as contested, because the figures are dated snapshots or use different cut-offs and units, so the passages do not oppose one proposition. New Delhi counts are kept as dated listing records; the HAIP counts are kept as context in the qualification of the record for the OECD paper’s list of 20. Confirm.
